compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional student committee, either person may speak up or help the group get back on topic. Familiarity with the agenda and responsibility for the meeting can explain who steps in.

The shared letters describe points of overlap: outward attention, interest in patterns and possibilities, and weight given to logical criteria. They do not determine how well either person runs a meeting.

The one letter difference concerns how someone tends to engage with the outside world. One approach gives the discussion a settled direction. Another leaves room for further information. Either person can use both.

### ENTJ and ENTP: two points of attention in the handover process

The committee has three weeks for nominations, eligibility review, public speeches, voting and handover. This is a fictional process, and the two fictional characters receive the same blank draft, the same deadline and the same candidates.

In the fictional handover, both organisers can work from the same required dates. One approach records a working timetable with a date for each step. Another keeps more than one feasible sequence open until the committee settles whether to add a question-and-answer session. Both approaches must meet the same deadline and eligibility rules.

Fixing dates tightly leaves little room when an eligibility dispute appears, so the notice has to be changed at short notice; rethinking the stages easily stretches the process, with the notice on its third version and voting day pushed back. The compromise is to fix three dates that should not move — nominations close, voting day, handover day — and leave the middle stages to one round of discussion.

What is worth checking afterwards is the process outcome: how many dates on the timetable are fixed, how many versions of the notice went out, how many eligibility appeals were filed, how entries compare with last year. Those numbers show where the process jammed; they cannot verify anyone's type, and who argued more elegantly in the meeting says nothing about the last letter either.

Both types are extraverted, so that outward process is dominant: Te for ENTJ and Ne for ENTP. The auxiliary is introverted and is the other kind of process: Ni for ENTJ and Ti for ENTP.

The Foundation’s overview lists the third process as Sensing for ENTJ and Feeling for ENTP, with both attitudes shown as options. This page uses Se and Fe. Boundary of use: the three scenes below are fictional, used only to tell two points of attention apart. Work is divided by task and actual experience, not by type; who watches the timetable and who watches the boundary of the rules depends on who knows, who is present and who normally owns that area.

### ENTJ and ENTP: the handover timetable — fixing dates and changing rules can run together

(Fictional scene) From the same three-week plan, one may write each checkpoint as a date and time, who submits, to whom, plus how a delay is handled; the other may write each checkpoint as what the stage is meant to solve and whether there is a cheaper way, then list two places that could merge.

The first risks having to make exceptions when something unexpected happens; the second risks a discussion with no end. The workable approach is not to decide whose version goes out first but to separate the two: the schedule goes out in one version, and any change is notified to everyone; rule-level changes are gathered into one round of discussion before nominations close, and anything after that goes into next year's review. That is a process arrangement, and it does not require deciding anyone's type first.

A schedule check can be done: draw the process as a timeline, mark the critical dependencies — which step, if unfinished, blocks which later ones — then mark the buffers (how many days between two checkpoints) and the fallbacks (what replaces a stage if it slips). Try a concrete case: if eligibility review slips a day, can the publication still go out on time? The answer is not in what proportion the word must occupies, but in whether dependencies were identified, whether the buffers are enough and whether fallbacks were written down in advance.

### ENTJ and ENTP: someone submits twenty minutes late

(Fictional scene) On the closing day for nominations, a candidate emails their material twenty minutes after the deadline. Both face the same notice, the same candidate and the same moment.

In this fictional case, both organisers consult the same notice to decide how to treat the application. Both can also record whether the form or announcement contributed to the delay. The first question concerns the current procedure. The second concerns what the committee might improve next time.

Both organisers apply the same published procedure. One could agree a timetable for responding; another could keep feasible response times open pending confirmation. Neither approach changes the eligibility rule, and either person can use either approach.

If late submissions keep recurring, the problem is usually not preference but the notification channel and the form design: what needs discussing is who sends the notice and where the template is easy to misread, not who is more principled.

### ENTJ and ENTP: a cousin says he wants to quit studying and learn a trade

(Fictional scene) The same disagreement is harder to raise at a relative's dinner table. A cousin says he cannot continue his vocational course and wants to learn car repair; his mother's eyes fill immediately.

One set of questions goes toward the cost and conditions of that path: how long the apprenticeship runs, roughly what a month pays once qualified, whether he could open his own workshop in three years — breaking the path into comparable years. The other goes toward where he is actually stuck: is it the classes or being managed, and which other paths have not been mentioned. Neither set is the property of one kind of person: the same person can ask about income and then ask what he cannot stand, and the reverse order works just as well.

Checking the conditions can help the student see what each route would involve. Exploring alternatives can uncover a route the student had not considered. Both questions matter, and the decision belongs to the student.

Ask the student what they want to change and what they would need to know before choosing. That can identify questions about training and daily work without turning the conversation into a type test.

compare_blocks.body:
Reading J as execution and P as procrastination is the most common mismatch. Someone who pulls three all-nighters for a speech may be on the perceiving side; someone who tears up an obviously unreasonable process may be on the judging side. Judging the last letter by reliability will almost certainly fail.

Interrupting or rejecting a proposal can reflect authority, time pressure or speaking habits. Neither action identifies J/P.

The third writes this pair as who is better suited to chairing or overall coordination. Scheduling and rule design are both trainable: someone who has run two rounds is practised at both, a newcomer at neither. A handover needs both, and the division should follow task and experience rather than four letters.

The fourth takes E for sociable. E means attention and energy turn outward more often; either type may not want to talk after a meeting, and either can organise a room full of people when needed.

If it shows a match score between two types, interpret it per that tool's scoring notes — closeness of a type-match score does not mean the J/P dimension score is also close.

Either way, there is no need to conclude that your preference is unstable, and no need to use a retest or meeting notes to adjudicate. A more useful move is to review whether you were answering from your own habit or from the requirements of the post at the time, and write that down.

Framework sources: preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/). These sources explain what the four preference letters mean and the basic idea of type dynamics; they do not supply the conclusions in the scenes here.

Four-position convention on this page: Te–Ni–Se–Fi for ENTJ and Ne–Ti–Fe–Si for ENTP follow the common in-site writing, in particular on whether the third process is marked extraverted, which tables handle differently; this is an editorial marking convention, not presented as the Foundation's only reading, and position order is not used to predict behaviour sequence, areas of strength or collaboration outcomes.

Editorial fiction note: the handover schedule, the late submission and the dinner-table discussion are editorial fiction, used to practise telling two points of attention apart, corresponding to no real person, organisation or event.

Scope limits: the number of notice versions, appeals and entries mentioned are process-review measures and cannot verify a type; this page is not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships.
